metadata.title: Control-value theory and enjoyment of science_ A cross-national investigation with 15-year-olds using PISA 2006 data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2006 microdata with a complex two-stage stratified sampling design (students nested within schools) across 57 countries. Following Rutkowski et al. (2010), the authors apply the standardized student weight to obtain unbiased population estimates and use a complex-design correction to adjust standard errors for the nesting of students within schools. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that the standardized student weight is used in all analyses. Because the analysis is conducted with Mplus using robust maximum likelihood, the weighting is used for population-representative estimation and correct standard errors rather than for any ML algorithmic weighting.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2006 full available international sample of 15-year-old students across 57 countries (398,750 students total). The study does not report additional task/module subsampling beyond using the PISA 2006 science literacy context questionnaire scales for perceived control (science self-concept items), personal value of science, utility value (instrumental motivation to learn school science), and enjoyment of science. Missing questionnaire responses were handled via multiple imputation (five imputed datasets) before model estimation. No explicit exclusion criteria (e.g., grade bands, school types, or booklet-based restrictions) are described beyond the standard PISA sampling and the use of the specified scale items.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) Science learning — enjoyment of science (context questionnaire)
top_predictors: Perceived control × Personal value of science
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM-LI Model 1 fit: χ2(146, N=398,750)=4678.2, CFI=0.986, TLI=0.983, RMSEA=0.009, SRMR=0.016. Interaction: β=0.042, SE=0.004, p<.001 (statistically significant but very small effect size).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) science learning the study leveraged perceived control (science self-concept) and personal value of science—plus their latent interaction—to predict enjoyment of science learning, finding that both main effects were positive and that the perceived control × personal value interaction was statistically significant (β=0.042, p<.001) but very small. This indicates that interventions should primarily strengthen students’ perceived control and personal relevance of science, while treating the synergistic interaction as a weak (not practically large) lever for increasing enjoyment, and causality cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional design.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-national study uses PISA 2006 microdata for 15-year-olds across 57 countries (398,750 students) to test Control-Value Theory in the science domain. Enjoyment of science learning is modeled as a latent outcome predicted by perceived control (science self-concept), value appraisals (personal value of science in Model 1; utility value of school science in Model 2), and their latent interaction using SEM with latent interactions (SEM-LI) estimated in Mplus with robust maximum likelihood. Multiple imputation was used for missing questionnaire responses (five imputed datasets via Amelia II). Model fit was strong for both models (Model 1: CFI=0.986, RMSEA=0.009; Model 2: CFI=0.983, RMSEA=0.010). The key interaction effects were statistically significant but very small (Model 1 β=0.042; Model 2 β=0.036), and the structural relations were largely invariant across countries and genders, though country-level patterns varied. Because the design is cross-sectional and the analysis is not causal, the findings support theory-consistent associations rather than causal effects.
